concepts.name: Origin and Evolution: FSF to FSB
key_dimensions: Financial Stability Forum (FSF) established in 1999 after Asian Financial Crisis vs FSB established in 2009 after Global Financial Crisis
Role of G20 Pittsburgh Summit 2009 in formally establishing FSB
Expansion of membership from G7-centric FSF to broader G20-inclusive FSB
Institutional continuity vs structural transformation between FSF and FSB

concepts.name: Legal Status and Institutional Character of FSB
key_dimensions: FSB as an international body without treaty-based legal personality (not a formal international organization)
Hosted by Bank for International Settlements (BIS) in Basel, Switzerland
Voluntary compliance mechanism — lacks binding enforcement powers
Transition from informal forum to association under Swiss law in 2013

concepts.name: Mandate and Core Objectives of FSB
key_dimensions: Promote international financial stability by coordinating national financial authorities and international standard-setting bodies
Monitor and make recommendations about the global financial system
Assess vulnerabilities in the global financial system and identify/oversee actions needed to address them
Distinction between FSB's coordination role vs IMF's surveillance/lending role

concepts.name: FSB Membership Structure and Composition
key_dimensions: Members include G20 national authorities (central banks, finance ministries, supervisory agencies), international financial institutions, and standard-setting bodies
International institutions: IMF, World Bank, BIS, OECD, ECB
Standard-setting bodies: BCBS, IOSCO, IAIS, IASB, CPMI
India's representation through RBI and Ministry of Finance; trap — India is a member but not all G20 economies have equal voting weight

concepts.name: FSB Governance Structure: Plenary, Steering Committee, and Chairs
key_dimensions: Plenary as the highest decision-making body meeting twice a year
Steering Committee for operational management between Plenary sessions
Standing Committees: SCAV (Assessment of Vulnerabilities), SCSN (Standards Implementation), SCSI (Supervisory and Regulatory Cooperation), RCGs (Regional Consultative Groups)
Chair appointed by G20 — distinction from IMF/World Bank where US has structural dominance

concepts.name: FSB's Role in Identifying Systemically Important Financial Institutions (SIFIs)
key_dimensions: Global Systemically Important Banks (G-SIBs) and Global Systemically Important Insurers (G-SIIs) designation
Annual publication of G-SIB list in coordination with BCBS
Higher Loss Absorbency (HLA) capital requirements for G-SIBs
Domestic SIFIs (D-SIBs) — FSB framework vs national regulators' discretion; India's D-SIBs (SBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank) designated by RBI

concepts.name: Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) Standard
key_dimensions: TLAC requires G-SIBs to hold minimum 16% of risk-weighted assets (rising to 18%) as loss-absorbing instruments
Distinction between TLAC (FSB standard for G-SIBs) vs MREL (EU's Minimum Requirement for Own Funds and Eligible Liabilities)
Purpose: ensure orderly resolution without taxpayer bailouts
Trap: TLAC is not the same as Basel III capital requirements — additive layer

concepts.name: FSB and Shadow Banking / Non-Bank Financial Intermediation (NBFI)
key_dimensions: FSB rebranded 'shadow banking' to 'Non-Bank Financial Intermediation (NBFI)' to reduce stigma
Annual Global Monitoring Report on NBFI tracking size and risks
Entities covered: money market funds, hedge funds, securitization vehicles, broker-dealers
Distinction: NBFI monitoring is FSB's role; direct regulation remains with national authorities and IOSCO

concepts.name: FSB's Key Vulnerability Assessments and Annual Reports
key_dimensions: Global Financial Stability Report (GFSR) is IMF's — not FSB's; FSB publishes Annual Report and vulnerability assessments
FSB's 'Vulnerabilities Affecting the Financial System' report to G20
Post-COVID focus on liquidity mismatches in open-ended funds and leverage in NBFIs
Crypto-asset risks — FSB's 2022–2023 framework for regulating crypto assets globally

concepts.name: FSB and Crypto-Asset Regulation Framework
key_dimensions: FSB's 2023 High-Level Recommendations for Regulation of Crypto-Asset Activities
'Same activity, same risk, same regulation' principle
FSB's separate framework for Global Stablecoins (GSCs) vs general crypto assets
Coordination with IOSCO, BCBS for implementation — FSB as coordinator, not direct regulator

concepts.name: FSB's Resolution Framework and Key Attributes
key_dimensions: 'Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes for Financial Institutions' (2011, updated 2014) — FSB's flagship standard
Bail-in vs bailout framework promoted by FSB post-2008 crisis
Cross-border cooperation in resolution — Crisis Management Groups (CMGs) for each G-SIB
Trap: FSB sets the standard; actual resolution authority rests with national resolution authorities

concepts.name: FSB's Relationship with BIS, IMF, and World Bank
key_dimensions: FSB is hosted by BIS but is legally independent of it (since 2013 Swiss law association)
IMF and World Bank are members of FSB Plenary but FSB reports to G20, not to IMF
Complementary roles: IMF does macro-financial surveillance; FSB does regulatory/supervisory coordination
Joint FSB-IMF Early Warning Exercise (EWE) presented to IMFC and G20 — overlap and distinction

concepts.name: FSB's OTC Derivatives Reforms
key_dimensions: G20 Pittsburgh 2009 commitment: OTC derivatives to be traded on exchanges/electronic platforms, cleared through CCPs, reported to trade repositories
FSB as monitor of implementation progress across jurisdictions
Central Counterparty (CCP) resilience, recovery, and resolution — FSB guidance
Trap: FSB monitors but IOSCO and CPMI set the specific CCP standards

concepts.name: FSB Peer Reviews and Implementation Monitoring
key_dimensions: Thematic Peer Reviews (e.g., on compensation practices, mortgage underwriting) vs Country Peer Reviews
Voluntary peer review mechanism — no sanctions for non-compliance
FSAP (Financial Sector Assessment Program) is joint IMF-World Bank — distinct from FSB peer reviews
India has undergone FSB peer reviews and FSAP assessments — both are different instruments

concepts.name: FSB and Climate-Related Financial Risks
key_dimensions: FSB established the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) in 2015
TCFD recommendations (2017) on governance, strategy, risk management, metrics/targets
Transition of TCFD to IFRS Foundation / ISSB in 2023 — FSB handed over monitoring role
Distinction: TCFD is a disclosure framework; not a prudential capital standard like Basel III

concepts.name: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) — Origins and Transition
key_dimensions: Created by FSB in 2015; chaired by Michael Bloomberg
Voluntary framework adopted by thousands of companies globally
ISSB (International Sustainability Standards Board) under IFRS Foundation absorbed TCFD in 2023
SEBI mandated BRSR (Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting) in India — aligned with TCFD principles

concepts.name: FSB Regional Consultative Groups (RCGs)
key_dimensions: Six RCGs covering Americas, Europe, Middle East and North Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, Commonwealth of Independent States
RCGs broaden FSB engagement beyond its 68 member institutions to non-member jurisdictions
India's role in FSB Asia RCG — awareness trap for UPSC on India's multilateral engagements
RCGs are consultative, not decision-making — recommendations flow upward to Plenary

concepts.name: FSB's Work on Cyber and Operational Resilience
key_dimensions: FSB Cyber Lexicon (2018) — common terminology for cyber risk in financial sector
Format for Incident Reporting Exchange (FIRE) — harmonized reporting framework (2023)
Coordination with BCBS Principles for Operational Resilience
Distinction: FSB sets coordination framework; sector-specific regulators (BCBS for banks, IOSCO for securities) set detailed rules

concepts.name: FSB's Annual G20 Reporting and Accountability Mechanism
key_dimensions: FSB Chair presents a letter to G20 Leaders' Summit annually outlining financial stability vulnerabilities
FSB work program is driven by G20 mandate — making FSB essentially a G20 body despite formal independence
Trap: FSB is not a G20 institution formally, but operationally derives its authority from G20 mandates
Comparison with Financial Action Task Force (FATF) — both are G20-linked standard setters but FATF has a blacklist/greylist enforcement mechanism; FSB does not

concepts.name: FSB vs FATF vs BCBS — Overlaps, Distinctions, and UPSC Traps
key_dimensions: FSB: financial stability coordination across all sectors; FATF: anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing; BCBS: banking prudential standards only
FATF has coercive listing mechanism (black/grey list); FSB and BCBS rely on peer pressure and market discipline
All three are hosted/connected to BIS ecosystem in Basel — trap on institutional location
FSB is a G20 body; FATF is an independent inter-governmental body; BCBS operates under BIS — legally distinct parentage
